en: The one early Neolithic settlement on Cyprus that is not on or near the coast. It sits in the hills about 25 km from the sea, and Alan Simmons of the University of Nevada dug it over campaigns from 1997 to 2018. Everything about it is awkward for the standard story: the architecture is unlike anything else on the island, the cattle bones are among the earliest directly dated domesticates anywhere in the Near East, and 982 marine shells were carried all the way up from the coast. It is the main reason the colonisation of Cyprus is no longer told as a story of coastal beachheads.

en: In situ; finds with the Department of Antiquities

One of only two places on Cyprus as old as the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A of the mainland, and the odd one of the pair: not a village but a working camp in the eastern Troodos foothills, where people made stone tools and ground red ochre. Carole McCartney's Elaborating Early Neolithic Cyprus project dug 203 square metres over five seasons up to 2013. The suggestion that its pigment was being produced partly for export back to the Levant turns the usual picture around, with Cyprus supplying the mainland rather than only receiving from it.

en: A ninth-millennium village on the north coast, and the place where Anatolian obsidian came ashore. Over four thousand pieces have been recorded here, more than every other Cypriot site put together, all of it finished bladelets from the Kömürcü-Kaletepe source in Cappadocia. Müge Sevketoglu ran rescue excavations from 2000 after building work began to destroy the site; less than five per cent of it has been dug. Its buildings had lime-plaster floors and painted plaster walls, and a broad ditch cut into bedrock runs across the excavated area.
The obsidian assemblage

More than four thousand pieces of Cappadocian obsidian, of which 3,600 have been catalogued. Over 95 per cent are finished bladelets, with almost no core waste, so the blades were made at the quarry in Anatolia and shipped across as a product. By comparison Shillourokambos has about 430 pieces, Ais Giorkis 42 and the Mylouthkia wells 8.

Standardised mudbricks
Bricks laid in regular courses, averaging 0.33 by 0.20 by 0.10 m and bonded with white plaster or gypsum mortar, so consistent in size that they suggest a standardised way of making them.
The animal bones

Fallow deer make up 45 per cent of the identified bones, sheep and goat 27 per cent and pig 17 per cent, while cattle amount to barely 2 per cent. The sheep and goats were killed young, as herders kill them; the deer were taken at all ages, as hunters take them.

en: A fishing hamlet clinging to a ledge on the steep flank of a limestone headland at the very tip of the Karpas, halfway between the plateau above and the sea below, in a position so awkward that it can only have been chosen for the water. Alain Le Brun's French mission dug it in three seasons between 1970 and 1973; the 1974 war ended the work and the site has since been badly damaged. Of all the Neolithic settlements on Cyprus this is the one that comes closest to being a genuine fishing village.
The small round houses

Circular dwellings only 2.5 to 2.8 m across, with thin dry-stone walls, hearths inside and storage bins set at floor level, some grouped around shared courtyards. They are the smallest Neolithic houses known on the island, a third the diameter of the largest at Khirokitia.

en: A large village of the Khirokitia culture on a vine-covered plateau above the lower Xeros Potamos, spotted by the Canadian archaeologist Bill Fox during the Palaipaphos survey in the 1980s and tested by Alan Simmons in 1993 and 1996. Ploughing has taken away the buildings, so Ortos is known almost entirely from pits and the material in the soil. Even so it ranks with Khirokitia and Kalavasos-Tenta among the larger settlements of its day, which is a warning about how many equally big villages have been quietly erased by farming.
The Ortos Head
c. 6000 BCE

A fist-sized head of grey diabase, 8.5 cm high, with chiselled brows, a flat vertical nose and a jutting chin, and diagonal lines engraved for what looks like a braided hairstyle. It is broken off just below the chin and was once part of a larger figure. Found on the surface in 1988.

en: In situ, under vines

A Ceramic Neolithic village on a prominent hill 243 m above sea level on the west bank of the Kouris, about 5 km inland. It was the first Cypriot field project of the University of Athens, dug by Eleni Mantzourani from 1992 to 1999 and published in full in 2009 and 2019, which makes it one of the best documented villages of the Sotira culture. Its two floor burials are the only ones of their kind in the whole period.
The burials under Building 15

Two pits cut into the floor of an apparently abandoned building held an adult man and a baby of about nine months. In the Aceramic Neolithic burying the dead under house floors was the rule; in the Ceramic Neolithic the dead were normally taken outside the village, and these two are the only known exceptions, which may say something about who they were.

A Ceramic Neolithic village on a low hillock right on the shore beside a natural harbour, excavated for the Department of Antiquities by Pavlos Flourentzos between 1995 and 2000. Around forty round and sub-rectangular houses stood on 3,250 square metres inside a horseshoe-shaped wall with two gates. If any Cypriot Neolithic site deserves to be called a fishing village it is this one, and yet three quarters of its meat came from hunted deer. An underwater survey published in 2025 has traced five drowned shorelines offshore, so how close to the water the village actually sat is now being reconsidered.
The horseshoe enclosure wall
c. 4500 BCE

A curved wall around the settlement with a main gate and a second on the south side, an unusual piece of communal building for the Ceramic Neolithic, when most villages were simply clusters of free-standing houses.

Some 77 per cent of the mammal bones are Mesopotamian fallow deer, which supplied roughly 90 per cent of the meat. A coastal village next to a harbour was living mainly by hunting an animal its ancestors had shipped to the island for exactly that purpose.

en: A hunters' camp high in the western Troodos, excavated by Nikolaos Efstratiou of Thessaloniki from 2011 and still under study. It matters for two reasons. It shows that the earliest Cypriots did not cling to the coast but went up into the mountains and adapted to them, shedding their maritime habits; and it helps fill the long blank in the record between the rock shelter at Aetokremnos and the first villages. Occupation was intermittent, with a later Aceramic Neolithic phase on top of the Epipalaeolithic one.

en: A Chalcolithic village of about four hectares on the coastal shelf north of Paphos, half destroyed by a 1970s land consolidation scheme that drove roads straight through it and then scheduled for building. The Department of Antiquities asked Leiden University to rescue what was left, and Bleda During's team has dug there with the University of Cyprus since 2015. A small, heavy blade 7.5 cm long weighing 119 grams, 99.5 per cent copper with a trace of tin. It is the only copper axe from a securely dated Chalcolithic context on Cyprus, has no Cypriot parallels, and matches flat axes from Horoztepe, Demircihuyuk and Thermi, so it was probably imported ready-made or cast from imported metal.

en: The buried jar and its contents

The axe was inside a large storage jar sunk into a lime-plaster surface, together with a broad basalt stone axe 12.7 cm long, four delicate fish hooks cut from pig tusk and a partly unrolled copper spiral. The excavators cannot decide between a hoard stashed for safekeeping and a deliberate ritual deposit, and lean towards the second.

en: Building 5

A roundhouse about eight metres across, its wall standing four courses high on a platform cut level into the bedrock, and one of the largest Chalcolithic buildings known. A flimsier successor, Building 6, was built partly from its robbed stones.
In situ, Chlorakas-Palloures
The burnt building

A house that burned down while stacked full of pots, stone tools and other combustible material. Its layer-by-layer study, published in 2022, is one of the few detailed accounts of how these fires actually happened.

en: The great pestle
A stone pestle 47 cm long, found with five other ground stone tools on a floor surface. Grinding at this scale suggests processing for more than one household.

en: Copper spiral
A strip of copper about 4 cm long and half a centimetre wide, coiled and partly unrolled, with a close parallel in the shaft graves at Souskiou.

A Bronze Age settlement barely a hundred metres from the Chalcolithic village at Mosphilia, dug since 2007 by Lindy Crewe for the Cyprus American Archaeological Research Institute. Occupied for some eight centuries, it covers exactly the stretch that western Cyprus is otherwise almost blank for: from the Philia horizon through to the end of the Middle Bronze Age. Its best-known feature is a domed mud-plaster structure argued to be a malting kiln.
The malting kiln

A domed mud-plaster chamber whose shape suits drying malt or curing malt cakes rather than firing pots or baking bread. A replica built by the site's field school was used to brew beer successfully, which supports the reading without proving it.

en: In situ, Kissonerga-Skalia
The monumental complex
About 1,600 square metres of planned building that required serious earthmoving and terracing, then went out of use after perhaps one or two generations.

en: Miniature cups and bowls
Middle to Late Bronze Age
Sets of tiny vessels deposited where one building phase gave way to the next, read as the remains of communal drinking at moments of rebuilding.

en: Plain White pithoi from eastern Cyprus
Big storage jars whose fabric belongs to the far side of the island, the clearest evidence yet that the west was inside an inter-island exchange network before the Late Bronze Age.

en: Deeply Incised and Red Polished wares
Locally made pottery covering the whole span of the village, including the deeply incised style that is a western regional signature.
